stance_basis: letter supports presidential ORV action but urges exclusion from wilderness/parks and recommends demonstration areas with close supervision
summary: L. W. True, Administrator of the Kentucky Program Development Office, submitted a letter supporting the presidential executive order directing federal agencies to establish ORV use policies, while also urging that ORV use be prohibited in wilderness, primitive areas, national parks, and wildlife refuges. He recommended opening certain lands on a demonstration basis under close supervision and suggested cooperation with manufacturers and parental guidance as complementary measures.
complaint_summary: L. W. True supports the presidential ORV action and federal policy-setting, but urges exclusion of ORV use from wilderness, primitive areas, national parks, and wildlife refuges, and recommends a demonstration-basis approach with close supervision for opening certain lands to ORV use.

statement.text:
It is apparent that Kentuckians are contributing to the national popularity of comparison and subsequent use of off-road vehicles (ORV). For comparison, our state licensing records reveal a four-fold increase in ORV licensing for use on public roadways since 1960, from 6,944 to 29,451. To license an ORV for such use the owner-operator must be at least 16 years of age. We have no indication of the number of vehicles not licensed. There is no evidence that their popularity may be leveling off.
ORV use in Kentucky State Parks is generally permitted on park roads open to automobile and camper traffic, within established safety regulations. ORV use in Kentucky State Forests is generally discouraged. The City of Louisville, Kentucky Park Board recently rescinded an earlier decision permitting ORV use in certain designated park areas because of serious destruction of the natural environment. The State Attorney General's Office has ruled that public park roads are in effect public roads, and therefore, state licensing requirements for ORV operation must be enforced. The operator under 16 years of age is placed at a certain disadvantage.
We definitely support recent presidential action directing federal agencies to establish policies regarding ORV use on their public lands. The increased popularity of the ORV accompanied by apparent pressure for a place to ride certainly warrants this action. By definition, ORV use must legitimately be given a position among outdoor recreation activities and must be considered in terms of total demand.
We further support the policy that ORV use not be permitted on wilderness or primitive areas, and we encourage the federal agency heads to recommend a similar policy for the national parks and national wildlife refuges and game areas. Since our federal govern-

ment already owns approximately 30 percent of all the land in the United States, and an even greater percentage in the Western United States, it would seem that sufficient land for ORV use could be located so as to not encroach upon parks and wildlife areas.
In the interim, until many of the questions can be resolved regarding the effects of ORV use on public lands, we suggest that consideration be given to opening certain lands to ORV use on a demonstration basis under close supervision and management. We also suggest that government leaders seek the cooperation of manufacturers concerning the operating features of the ORV. However, there is really no substitute for parental guidance and restraint in the teenager's selection of an ORV, with individual as well as the public interest in mind.
Thank you for the opportunity to review the subject environmental statement. We certainly want to be kept up-to-date on the policies established regarding ORV use on federal lands. If further state coordination is desired this office will be pleased to provide assistance.
Sincerely yours,
L. W. True
Administrator
